## Why This Is Asked
This probes certificate rotation in CKAD scope without relying on cert-manager, exercising a real-world secret lifecycle, Ingress TLS updates, and constrained network egress.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped CronJob and Secrets
- TLS certificate rotation without a controller
- Ingress TLS secret refresh
- InitContainer tooling installation
- NetworkPolicy egress controls

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton for the CronJob
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: tls-rotator
spec:
  schedule: "*/15 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: tls-rotator
            image: bundle/curl-jq
            command: ["sh", "-c", "fetch && update-secret && update-ingress"]
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

- How would you verify the secret rotation is applied across dependent pods?
- What failure modes require manual intervention and how would you detect them?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests knowledge of namespace-scoped governance primitives (LimitRange, ResourceQuota) and how defaults affect scheduling, QoS, and multi-tenant fairness in CKAD.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace scoping
- LimitRange defaultRequests/defaultLimits
- ResourceQuota hard limits
- Pod scheduling under quotas
- Impact on autoscaling and experimentation

## Code Example
```yaml
# Namespace
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: test-ns
---
# LimitRange
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
  namespace: test-ns
spec:
  limits:
  - default:
      cpu: 200m
      memory: 256Mi
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: 100m
      memory: 128Mi
    type: Container
---
# ResourceQuota
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: resource-quota
  namespace: test-ns
spec:
  hard:
    pods: "10"
    requests.cpu: "1"
    requests.memory: 1Gi
    limits.cpu: "2"
    limits.memory: 2Gi
---
# Deployment (inherits defaults)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: sample-app
  namespace: test-ns
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: sample-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: sample-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:latest
```

## Trade-offs
**Advantages:**
- Prevents resource starvation across namespaces
- Enforces fair resource distribution
- Automatic defaults reduce configuration errors
- Provides cost control boundaries

**Considerations:**
- Too restrictive limits can hinder scaling
- Default limits may be overprovisioned for small workloads
- ResourceQuota refusals require manual quota increases
- May impact autoscaling behavior if quotas are too tight

**Best Practices:**
- Set conservative defaults but allow overrides
- Monitor quota utilization regularly
- Use separate quotas for production vs development
- Consider pod priority classes for critical workloads

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests your ability to design an isolated audit pattern with in-cluster API access, RBAC scoping, and security boundaries.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped RBAC for fine-grained access control
- In-cluster API access using Secrets and ConfigMaps
- PVC-backed persistent logs and InitContainers for tooling
- NetworkPolicy for egress control to restrict traffic to the collector
- Health checks (readiness/liveness probes) for reliability

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: audit-baseline
  namespace: example
data:
  baseline.json: |
    {"pods": [], "services": []}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: audit-auth
  namespace: example
type: Opaque
stringData:
  token: " collector-auth-token"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: audit-logs
  namespace: example
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: audit-agent
  namespace: example
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: audit-agent
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: audit-agent
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: installer
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl jq && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tools
          mountPath: /tools
      containers:
      - name: auditor
        image: your-audit-image:latest
        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "while true; do audit.sh; sleep 60; done"]
        env:
        - name: COLLECTOR_URL
          value: "http://collector.audit-system.svc.cluster.local:8080"
        - name: AUTH_TOKEN
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: audit-auth
              key: token
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
        - name: tools
          mountPath: /tools
        - name: baseline
          mountPath: /baseline
          readOnly: true
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /ready
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: audit-logs
      - name: tools
        emptyDir: {}
      - name: baseline
        configMap:
          name: audit-baseline
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: audit-egress-restrict
  namespace: example
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: audit-agent
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: audit-system
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: collector
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080
```

## Trade-offs
- **Pros**: Namespace isolation ensures audit agents don't interfere; NetworkPolicy provides security; PVC enables log persistence for compliance
- **Cons**: Each namespace requires separate Deployment (use Operator/Controller to automate); InitContainer adds startup latency; per-namespace RBAC management overhead increases with cluster size

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests the ability to compose CKAD primitives into a small, observable application with proper security and observability patterns.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMaps and Secrets for configuration management
- InitContainers and Sidecars for application lifecycle management
- Probes (readiness and liveness) for health monitoring
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for traffic security
- RBAC basics for in-namespace metrics access
- Observability and security trade-offs in containerized applications

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal Deployment sketch
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: python-api
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: python-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: python-api
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-deps
        image: python:3.11-alpine
        command: ['sh', '-c', 'pip install -r /app/requirements.txt']
        volumeMounts:
        - name: app-code
          mountPath: /app
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: python:3.11-alpine
        command: ['python', '/app/main.py']
        env:
        - name: ENABLE_METRICS
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: app-config
              key: ENABLE_METRICS
        - name: API_USERNAME
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: api-credentials
              key: username
        - name: API_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: api-credentials
              key: password
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
        volumeMounts:
        - name: app-code
          mountPath: /app
      - name: cert-rotator
        image: cert-manager/cert-manager-rotator:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: certs
          mountPath: /etc/certs
      volumes:
      - name: app-code
        configMap:
          name: app-code
      - name: certs
        emptyDir: {}
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-egress
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: monitoring
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 9000
```

## Trade-offs
- **Security vs. Complexity**: NetworkPolicy adds security but increases deployment complexity
- **Resource Overhead**: Sidecar containers double resource requirements for cert management
- **Observability Cost**: Metrics endpoint requires additional monitoring infrastructure
- **InitContainer Impact**: Dependency installation extends pod startup time
- **Namespace Isolation**: Per-namespace design improves security boundaries but requires duplicate configuration management

## Why This Is Asked
Tests CKAD-level design and debugging of StatefulSets, bootstrapping, and network policies under real constraints.

## Key Concepts
- StatefulSet with stable identity and PVC
- headless Service and partitioned rolling updates
- InitContainer for bootstrapping
- PodDisruptionBudget and readiness/liveness probes
- Resource quotas and NetworkPolicy bounds

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: cache-svc
  labels:
    app: cache
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: cache
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: cache
spec:
  serviceName: cache-svc
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cache
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cache
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: seed
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh", "-c", "echo seed > /data/.seed"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
      containers:
      - name: cache
        image: redis:7
        ports:
        - containerPort: 6379
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: "/ready", port: 6379}
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: "/live", port: 6379}
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: cache-pvc
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: cache
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: cache-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cache
```

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests practical CKAD skills, including permissioning, automation, and Kubernetes-native policy enforcement using a CronJob with ConfigMap-driven behavior.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped CronJob for periodic enforcement
- ConfigMap-driven policy configuration (imageRepo, imageTag)
- kubectl patch or server-side apply for image updates
- PVC-based logging and HTTP POST for audit trails
- InitContainer for tooling installation (curl, jq)
- Namespace NetworkPolicy scoping for egress control

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: image-tag-enforcer
  namespace: default
spec:
  schedule: "*/5 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
          - name: installer
            image: busybox
            command: ["sh", "-c", "apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl jq"]
          containers:
          - name: enforcer
            image: curlimages/curl:latest
            command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
            args:
            - |
              # Read policy from ConfigMap
              # Get all Deployments in namespace
              # Compare images against policy
              # Patch mismatched Deployments
              # Write heartbeat log to /logs
              # POST summary to policy-portal
            volumeMounts:
            - name: log-volume
              mountPath: /logs
            readinessProbe:
              exec:
                command: ["test", "-f", "/logs/ready"]
              initialDelaySeconds: 5
              periodSeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:
              exec:
                command: ["test", "-f", "/logs/alive"]
              initialDelaySeconds: 15
              periodSeconds: 20
          volumes:
          - name: log-volume
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: enforcer-logs
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-egress
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: policy-portal
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080
```

## Trade-offs
- **Frequency**: Running every 5 minutes balances responsiveness vs. resource usage; longer intervals reduce API load but delay remediation
- **PVC vs. Sidecar**: Using a PVC is simpler but requires storage provisioning; a sidecar could stream logs directly
- **Patch vs. Reconcile Controller**: A declarative controller would be more robust but requires custom operator development; CronJob is quicker to implement but imperative
- **InitContainer**: Pre-installing tools increases pod startup time; consider using a custom image with tools baked in instead
- **NetworkPolicy**: Restricting egress improves security but may break legitimate communication; ensure all required endpoints are explicitly allowed
- **Idempotency**: Multiple enforcers running simultaneously could cause conflicts; consider adding a lock mechanism or using `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid`

## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates practical Kubernetes operational skills including StatefulSet storage migration, configuration change propagation, health monitoring, security hardening, and availability guarantees during disruptions.

## Key Concepts
- PersistentVolumeClaim integration with StatefulSets and StorageClass selection
- ConfigMap checksum annotations for automated rolling updates
- Health probe configuration (readiness vs liveness)
- Pod security context with non-root execution and file system permissions
- PodDisruptionBudget for maintaining service availability
- Load testing strategies and rollback procedures

## Code Example
```yaml
# Strategic merge patch
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: collector
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsUser: 1000
        runAsGroup: 1000
        fsGroup: 1000
      containers:
      - name: collector
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "100m"
          limits:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /livez
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /var/lib/collector
        - name: config
          mountPath: /etc/collector
      volumes:
      - name: config
        configMap:
          name: collector-config
          items:
          - key: config
            path: config
        annotations:
          checksum/config: "{{ .Values.configChecksum }}"
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: data
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      storageClassName: "fast-ssd"
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 10Gi
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: collector-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: collector
```

## Verification Strategy
Monitor rollout progress: `kubectl rollout status statefulset/collector -n telemetry`
Validate pod health: `kubectl get pods -n telemetry -l app=collector -w`
Check PVC binding: `kubectl get pvc -n telemetry`
Load test using k6 or hey targeting collector endpoints
Verify ConfigMap changes trigger restarts by updating ConfigMap and watching pod recreation

## Rollback Approach
Use `kubectl rollout undo statefulset/collector -n telemetry` for immediate rollback
For complex issues, restore from previous StatefulSet manifest and scale down/up
Always validate PDB compliance during rollback to avoid availability violations

- **Sidecar overhead**: TLS rotation adds reliability but increases resource consumption
